inputs.original_text: Abinader’s government has signed an agreement in Paris with OECD chief Mathias Cormann to design the Dominican Republic’s first National Integrity and Anti-Corruption Strategy. Corruption isn’t an abstract governance problem: it drains resources and weakens services people rely on, especially those with the least power. But international standards won’t fix that on their own. The real measure is whether Dominican institutions become more accountable to the public and whether reform challenges entrenched power—not simply whether the government adopts a framework designed with international officials.
inputs.modified_text: Abinader’s government has signed an agreement in Paris with OECD chief Mathias Cormann to design the Dominican Republic’s first National Integrity and Anti-Corruption Strategy. That matters because corruption shifts public resources away from services people depend on, with the greatest harm falling on those who already have the least power. But an international framework is no substitute for confronting the institutions and entrenched interests that allow corruption to persist. The test is whether ordinary people gain real power to hold officials accountable—not whether the government can announce a strategy.
